newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: IRA reported to be observing unofficial truce.
newsitem.headline: IRA reported to be observing unofficial truce.

text.p: The IRA is observing an unofficial truce in its guerrilla war against Britain to win better terms for the entry of its Sinn Fein political wing into Northern Ireland peace talks, Dublin's Sunday Tribune newspaper reported.

The newspaper said the Irish Republican Army guerrillas had observed the truce since they bombed Britain's Northern Ireland army base at Lisburn, outside Belfast, killing one soldier and injuring 30 on October 7.

The aim of the truce was to enhance mediation efforts between Sinn Fein and the British and Irish governments by John Hume, leader of Northern Ireland's Social, Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), the newspaper said.

Hume acknowledged this month that he was holding talks with Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams to try to get the IRA to restore a 17-month truce it broke in February with a bombing campaign in Britain, Germany and the Lisburn attack.

The British and Irish governments have banned all ministerial contact with Sinn Fein since the ending of the IRA ceasefire and say that only a new truce will allow Sinn Fein to join other parties at peace talks under way in Belfast.

Senior figures in the Irish republican movement, which seeks to end British rule of Northern Ireland and reunite the province with Ireland, were predicting renewed violence unless the talks' terms were eased, the newspaper said.
There was no immediate comment on the report from either the British or Irish governments, which are due to review the Northern Ireland peace process on Wednesday.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, and Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, will meet in Belfast to discuss the talks, which started, without Sinn Fein, last June.

The Tribune said the IRA observed several similar unofficial ceasefires in the run-up to an August 1994 "total cessation" of its guerrilla war which helped open the door to the most intense effort to end the Northern Ireland conflict in 27 years.
The Tribune report followed media speculation that the IRA was considering calling a new truce if the two governments gave specific assurances on how the talks would be conducted.
It also followed speeches last week by Mayhew and Sinn Fein's key strategist, Martin McGuinness, which were seen as coded dialogue about what each side expected from the other.
Mayhew said an IRA truce would have to be matched by deeds if Britain was to have any faith in a new ceasefire. The London government wants assurances that a new truce will be permanent.

McGuinness said that Sinn Fein would not try to secure a new IRA truce unless Britain set a credible time-frame for the talks and dropped what he said were preconditions aimed at getting the IRA to surrender its guerrilla arsenal.
Sin Fein's arch-foes, Protestant Unionist parties which want the province to stay British, insist that the IRA must agree to surrender arms to prove a commitment to democratic means.

Under the terms of the talks, participants must pledge loyalty to a set of principles on non-violence and democracy and Unionists, which represent the province's 60 percent Protestant majority, insist that this means a surrender of weapons.

Parties to the talks have agreed that guerrillas must hand over weapons as the negotiations progress but the IRA says this cannot happen until there is a final political settlement to a conflict that has killed 3,200 people.
